© NASA / JPL-Caltech — U.S. Government work, public domain. Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object — about 170 AU from the Sun and travelling at ~17 km/s relative to it. Saturn is the catalogued destination because Voyager 1's mission profile ended there; its Titan flyby (1980-11-12) bent the trajectory upward out of the ecliptic plane, and after that no further planetary encounter was possible. The spacecraft crossed the heliopause on 2012-08-25 — the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. Pale Blue Dot family photograph taken 1990-02-14 from a heliocentric distance of ~6 billion km. Mission planning credit: Gary Flandro, JPL, who identified the late-1970s outer-planet alignment that made the Grand Tour possible.

Cape Canaveral, 1977-09-05. Launched 16 days AFTER Voyager 2 but on a higher-energy direct trajectory that overtakes its twin en route to Jupiter. Gary Flandro's Grand Tour mission profile exploits a late-1970s outer-planet alignment that won't recur for ~175 years; the chemical engine alone can't reach Saturn, so Jupiter's gravity does the bending.

Closest approach 348,890 km from Jupiter's centre (about 280,000 km above the cloud tops) on 1979-03-05. The encounter discovers Jupiter's rings, captures Io's active volcanism (Linda Morabito's chance pixel), and maps the magnetic-field structure that traps the Io plasma torus. Jupiter's gravity bends and speeds Voyager 1 on to Saturn, set up for Titan's haze at Saturn 21 months later.

Closest approach 124,000 km from Saturn on 1980-11-12; the same day, about 18 hours earlier, Voyager 1 passes within 6500 km of Titan to probe its nitrogen haze. The Titan-targeted geometry bends the trajectory 35° upward out of the ecliptic plane, ending any future planetary encounter — Voyager 1 is now committed to interstellar space. Heliopause crossing followed on 2012-08-25; the spacecraft is the most distant human-made object.
Most distant human-made object — currently ~170 AU from the Sun in interstellar space

Voyager 1 is the farthest thing humanity has ever made, and it got there almost by an accident of geometry. A close pass by Saturn’s giant moon Titan — chosen for the science — bent its path up and out of the plane of the planets and aimed it at the edge of the solar system, and it has been climbing ever since. Along the way it found active volcanoes on Io, the first ever seen off Earth, and in 1990 it turned back to take the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it became the first machine to cross into interstellar space. It is still transmitting, on fading nuclear power, from more than a hundred times the Earth’s distance from the Sun.

Launched 16 days after Voyager 2, Voyager 1 flew faster and arrived at Jupiter first (1979) and Saturn first (1980). Its Titan flyby bent the trajectory upward out of the ecliptic plane, ending the planetary tour but sending it on the most direct path to the heliopause — which it crossed on 2012-08-25, the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. From a heliocentric distance of ~6 billion km it took the Pale Blue Dot family portrait (1990-02-14), the photograph Carl Sagan wrote about. Both Voyagers carry the Golden Record as humanity’s calling card.
